issues.issue: 'Neither the Term ... nor Network Operator's obligations ... shall be deemed to have expired or terminated until the services transfer assistance ... is completed' has no outer limit and no definition of completion.

This open-ended extension cannot be squared with Section 3.1, under which the Term terminates on the tenth anniversary of the Commencement Date, nor with the termination rights in Sections 8.1 and 8.6.
'services transfer assistance, as described herein' is never actually described beyond a duty to 'cooperate', so the content of the obligation is unstated.
Assistance may be required 'upon any notice of termination or of non-renewal of the Agreement pursuant to ARTICLE 3', but Article 3 contains no notice of termination mechanism.

'the effective date of such expiration or termination shall be extended for up to one year' at MTC's request gives one Party a unilateral power to prolong the contract without stating the terms of payment.
A unilateral one-year extension cannot be squared with Section 3.1's fixed Term or with Section 3.2's requirement that renewal be by mutual agreement.
'on mutually acceptable terms and conditions' makes the transfer obligation an agreement to agree, and 'other necessary third party services' is an undefined catch-all after the enumerated examples.

The Operator's right to terminate for MTC's material breach sits against Section 8.4.1, under which its obligations are not deemed terminated until transfer assistance is complete, and Section 11.2's duty of continued performance.

Limb (d) covers any act or omission that causes 'in whole or in part' MTC to breach an agreement with 'any other person relating to the MTC Network', a general catch-all following specific categories of counterparty.
The indemnity runs to 'Affiliates, officers, directors ... successors and assigns' as Indemnified Parties, which sits against Section 12.11's provision that no rights are conferred on non-parties.
MTC's indemnity is markedly narrower than the Operator's under Section 9.1, omitting bodily injury and infringement, so the asymmetry may be argued as deliberate expressio unius.

'So long as the Indemnifying Party is not in default in the performance of its obligations under the Agreement' conditions control of the defence on a default test that is nowhere confined to material default.
Apportionment on 'final adjudication' assumes a court judgment, while Section 11.1.3 makes arbitration a condition precedent to any suit and the arbitrator's award final.
Requiring 'the written approval of both the Parties' for any settlement gives the indemnified Party a veto without any reasonableness qualification.
Section 9.3 gives the Indemnifying Party 'primary responsibility for the conduct of an Indemnified Claim Proceeding', which is hard to square with a mutual settlement veto here.

'and such other coverages as the Parties may determine are commercially reasonable' is an open-ended addition to a carefully enumerated schedule, and 'As and when required' in 10.1.2 leaves the automobile trigger unstated.
Section 10.1.3 requires contractual liability cover only for indemnity obligations under Sections 9.1(a), 9.1(d) and 9.1(e), leaving 9.1(b) and 9.1(c) uninsured though still owed.
'The Parties will confer ... to determine commercially reasonable levels and types of coverage' leaves the property insurance obligation to future agreement with no fallback.
Section 5.1.16 warrants that the Operator 'has taken out all insurance required under this Agreement' as of the Effective Date, which cannot be true of coverage still to be agreed under this Section.
'insuring against all standard perils ... (subject to normal and customary terms, exclusions, sublimits and conditions)' both grants and takes away by reference to undefined market practice.
'in any other sequence of Losses' uses the capitalised term 'Losses', which is not defined in Article 2 or anywhere in the Agreement.
'Where possible' and 'an annual aggregate limit commensurate with the value of the assets in service' leave the required limit unascertainable.
'commercially reasonable deductibles reasonably satisfactory to MTC' combines an objective and a subjective standard without saying which governs.
'so-called "all risk" and "law and ordinance" coverage' incorporates market terms of art whose content is not fixed by the Agreement.
Section 10.2.2 already requires All Risk coverage 'subject to normal and customary ... exclusions', while this Section requires cover 'without limitation' of the listed perils.
'Subject to such further determination as to commercially reasonable amounts, timing, deductibles, and terms' makes the rental loss cover contingent on later agreement.

Section 2.45 treats rental loss proceeds as Network Revenue and Section 4.11.8.2 nets recovery costs from them, so the cover this Section leaves to future agreement drives fixed revenue-share obligations.
'other statutory insurances where it would be inappropriate' is an undefined exception to the additional insured requirement.

The additional-insured requirement is limited to 'the policies listed in Section 10.1', although Section 10.3.4 assumes property policies under Section 10.2 are also within the same regime by naming MTC as loss payee.
A blanket waiver of recovery against MTC sits against Section 9.2, under which MTC indemnifies the Operator for losses from MTC's third-party breaches and non-compliance with law.
The certificate deadlines are internally muddled: complete policies are due within thirty days of the Effective Date 'or policy renewal date', while certificates are due thirty days before expiry.
The opening carve-out 'Except as set forth in Section 10.2.1' points to a provision that says nothing about certificates, and Section 8.1.1 makes a breach of this Section a ten-day cure default.
'a reasonable administrative fee as designated by MTC' lets one Party set its own charge, and 'documenting commercially reasonable types and amounts' of subcontractor insurance fixes no level.

MTC is to be 'named as loss payee' on property policies here, while Section 10.3 limits the additional-insured endorsement to the Section 10.1 liability policies and Section 4.11.8.1 directs proceeds to repair.
The declared refusal to limit the Operator's liability sits against Section 12.14, which caps the parent guaranty at $4,000,000.

The cross-reference to 'agreements between MTC and others that are within the scope of Section 4.1' is astray, since agreements between MTC and third parties are the subject of Section 4.9.2, not Section 4.1.

'Any dispute between the Parties either with respect to the interpretation of any provision ... or with respect to the performance' fixes the scope of a mandatory dispute regime, and the closing words 'regardless of whether or not mention of this Article is made in any other Section' extend it to matters not expressly referred.

Because 'Party' is defined in Section 2.50 as only MTC and the Network Operator, this clause does not reach the parent guarantor whose guaranty Section 12.14 requires, leaving the forum for guaranty disputes unresolved.
'appropriate and germane' sets no standard for what information the IPT must gather and furnish.
The duty to meet 'as often as necessary' sits against Section 6.1.3, under which the IPT need meet only once a year.
The IPT is only to 'discuss the problem and negotiate in good faith' here, while Section 6.1.1(iv) states that its purpose includes resolving disputes submitted under Article 11.
'all reasonable requests ... for non-privileged information reasonably related to the Agreement, will be honored' is a disclosure duty with no stated limit or timeframe.
The obligation to honour information requests sits against the confidentiality restrictions of Article 7 and Section 9.4's express subjection of records to those limits.
The escalation runs from 'receipt by the other Party of the Dispute Resolution Notice', so the fifteen-day and thirty-day periods overlap and the officers' window shrinks to fifteen days.
Section 11.1.3 then measures the arbitration trigger from forty-five days after the same notice, so the three deadlines in Article 11 all run from one date and must be harmonised.

'Except in the case of an emergency, exhaustion of the foregoing procedures shall be a condition precedent' leaves 'emergency' undefined, and the clause both makes arbitration a condition precedent to any suit and carves out 'applications to courts of competent jurisdiction for injunctive relief'.

The clause binds only 'the Parties' as defined in Section 2.50, so its application to the parent guaranty required by Section 12.14 — and its interaction with Section 11.1.4's court route and Section 11.2's continued performance duty — is left open.
'would permit or cause irreparable injury ... due to delay arising out of the dispute resolution process' is a self-judging condition on immediate resort to court.

This open court route cannot easily be squared with Section 11.1.3, which makes arbitration a condition precedent to 'any suit, action or proceeding instituted in any court', subject only to a narrower injunctive-relief carve-out.
'unless otherwise directed by MTC' allows one Party unilaterally to suspend the other's performance obligations while a dispute is pending, without limit or standard.
A duty to keep performing 'while the dispute is being resolved' cannot easily be squared with the termination rights in Sections 8.1 and 8.6 or with Section 8.4.1's transfer-assistance regime.
The merger clause is limited to 'the Services and matters addressed therein', leaving open what other agreements between these Parties survive.

The clause sits against Section 12.14's parent guaranty, Section 4.13.1's yet-to-be-completed SLA and Section 4.7.4.1's incorporation of Network Policies, all of which are documents outside the signed text.
'Time is of the essence' is stated without qualification alongside an excuse for nonperformance caused by the other Party, leaving the two rules to be reconciled.
The excuse is limited to 'nonmonetary obligations', which sits against Section 4.9.2.8's monetary reduction for MTC-caused delay and Section 4.1.11's adjustment of deliverable dates.

'any other provisions that by their terms cannot be performed prior to the expiration or earlier termination' is a general catch-all following two named Articles, so which other provisions survive is contestable.
Article 3.6's post-term dark fiber rights, Article 7's post-termination confidentiality duties and Section 8.4's transfer assistance are all intended to survive but are not among the named survivors.
'such provision shall be deemed to be restated to reflect the Parties' original intentions as nearly as possible' invites a court to rewrite rather than sever an invalid term.

The choice of Massachusetts law for 'any and all claims and disputes arising out of ... the relationships and arrangements between MTC and Network Operator' overlaps with Section 11.1.3's own choice-of-law direction to the arbitrator, and neither addresses the parent guaranty required by Section 12.14.

The permitted assignees are 'another entity of the Commonwealth, a subsidiary of MTC or a special purpose entity', but the notice sentence then speaks of assignment 'to an Affiliate', a different and undefined class here.

The bar on assignment without consent sits against Section 4.7.3, which effects a present assignment of Third Party Service Provider contracts to MTC on termination, and against Section 8.5.1's transfer obligations.

The bar on third-party rights cannot easily be squared with Section 2.24 and Article 9, which confer indemnity rights on Affiliates, officers and directors, or with Section 10.3's naming of MassDOT and its bond trustees as additional insureds.
Limb (e) — 'when received electronically if sent by email and one of the delivery methods in (a) through (d) above' — is garbled and does not say whether email alone is ever effective.
Section 4.2.4 permits acceptance-test challenges to be 'transmitted electronically', which sits against a notice clause that appears to require email to be paired with another method.

A general duty not to withhold consent unreasonably sits against provisions giving MTC 'sole discretion' (Sections 2.7 and 4.9.7) and against Section 4.5.3's grounds for refusing approval of the Fiber Management Plan.

The proviso 'that Network Operator shall be subject to any application or access fees and that such policies and procedures MassDOT has agreed with MTC to apply in a non-discriminatory manner' is ungrammatical and appears to have dropped a negative, so it reads against the interest the proviso was meant to protect.

The final sentence makes it 'the sole responsibility of Network Operator to obtain all governmental approvals for any Alterations to be done by or on behalf of MTC', which cannot be squared with Section 4.2.1's allocation of permitting responsibility to MTC and its vendors.

'use all reasonable efforts to limit the rights and obligations of Network Operator so that it does not become a subrecipient of the Grant' sets an aim that could require cutting back rights and duties conferred elsewhere, without saying which.

The direction to limit the Operator's rights and obligations sits against the extensive fixed obligations of Article 4 and the dark fiber rights of Section 3.6, and against Section 12.1's rule that changes require a signed writing.

'This Agreement shall become binding only upon condition that' the parent delivers a guaranty 'in a form acceptable to MTC' leaves both the condition's satisfaction and the guaranty's terms to MTC's later judgment.

The guaranty is a separate instrument whose disputes are not obviously caught by Article 11, which covers only disputes 'between the Parties' as defined in Section 2.50, and Section 12.11 denies rights to non-parties.
